body:
Meaning of fermentation

Fermentation is a process in which microorganisms or their enzymes convert food substances, especially sugars, into other substances such as organic acids, alcohol or gases.

Fermentation is a chemical change because new substances are formed. It can alter the flavour, texture and keeping qualities of food.

Microorganisms do not all produce the same fermentation products. The result depends on the type of organism, the food material and the conditions under which the process occurs.

Formation of curd from milk

Role of lactic acid bacteria

Lactobacillus and other lactic acid bacteria help convert milk into curd. These beneficial bacteria use milk sugars and produce lactic acid.

The acid lowers the pH of milk and causes milk proteins, especially casein, to coagulate. This gives curd its characteristic thicker consistency and sour taste.

A small quantity of existing curd may be used as a starter culture. It introduces the useful bacteria into fresh milk, where they can multiply under suitable conditions.

The important chemical product in curd formation is lactic acid, not ethyl alcohol.

Fermentation by yeast

Production of alcohol and carbon dioxide

Yeast is a fungus. A commonly used baking and fermentation yeast is Saccharomyces cerevisiae.

Under suitable conditions, yeast converts sugars into ethanol, also called ethyl alcohol, and carbon dioxide. This is known as alcoholic fermentation.

The relationship can be expressed simply as:

Sugar becomes ethyl alcohol and carbon dioxide through the action of yeast.

Why bread dough rises

When yeast acts on suitable sugars in dough, the carbon dioxide produced becomes trapped as gas bubbles. These bubbles expand the dough and give it a lighter, porous structure.

Therefore, the main reason for the rising of yeast-fermented bread dough is the formation and retention of carbon dioxide gas. The yeast is not producing oxygen to raise the dough.

Fermentation of idli and dosa batter

Traditional idli and dosa batter is prepared from ingredients such as rice and pulses. Naturally occurring or introduced microorganisms, especially bacteria together with yeasts in some preparations, ferment the batter.

Fermentation produces acids and gases. The acids help develop the characteristic flavour, while gas formation contributes to the lightness of the batter. These changes are particularly important for preparing soft idlis.

Fermented batters are also used in some traditional forms of Gujarati dhokla. However, some instant dhokla preparations rely on chemical raising agents instead of a prolonged microbial fermentation stage. The names of the foods alone do not establish that the same method has been used.

Fermentation and food preservation

Fermentation can help preserve certain foods when useful microorganisms produce enough acid or other inhibitory substances to suppress many unwanted microbes. For example, suitable lactic acid fermentation increases acidity.

However, fermented does not automatically mean safe. Controlled conditions, suitable ingredients and hygienic handling remain important.

Fermented pickles and vinegar-added pickles

The term pickle does not always mean fermented food.

  • Fermented pickle: Beneficial microorganisms produce acid from substances in the food during fermentation.
  • Vinegar-added pickle: Acetic acid is supplied directly by vinegar. A quick-process vinegar pickle may be prepared without fermentation.

Both can be acidic, but the source of the acid is different.

How vinegar itself is produced

Vinegar production can involve 2 biological stages. Yeast first converts suitable sugars into alcohol. Acetic acid bacteria, including organisms of the genus Acetobacter, can then convert ethanol into acetic acid in the presence of oxygen.

This also illustrates why the oxygen requirements of different microbial processes should not be assumed to be identical.

Fermentation compared with other changes

ProcessWhat happensMain distinction
Milk fermentationLactic acid bacteria produce acidMilk becomes curd
Yeast fermentationYeast produces ethanol and carbon dioxideGas can raise bread dough
PasteurisationControlled heat reduces microorganismsMicroorganisms are not deliberately grown
Unwanted food spoilageUncontrolled changes may occurFood quality or safety deteriorates

Prelims focus

  • Lactobacillus is associated with the conversion of milk into curd.
  • Lactic acid helps coagulate milk proteins during curd formation.
  • Saccharomyces cerevisiae is a commonly used yeast.
  • Carbon dioxide produced during yeast fermentation makes bread dough rise.
  • Traditional idli and dosa batters undergo microbial fermentation.
  • Trap: A vinegar-added pickle need not have undergone fermentation.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 2, Microorganisms: Friend and Foe, sections 2.3 and Commercial Use of Microorganisms, printed pp. 19–20; NCERT, Biology, Class 12, Chapter 10, Microbes in Human Welfare, sections 10.1–10.2; National Center for Home Food Preservation, General Information on Fermenting, section on fermented and quick-process pickles, consulted 3 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Lactic acid sets milk into curd, trapped carbon dioxide raises bread dough, and acids and gases give fermented batter flavour and lightness.
pictures.caption: Different microorganisms produce different food changes.

title: Fermentation: Useful Microorganisms in Everyday Foods

What is rusting?

Iron objects left exposed to moist air may gradually develop a reddish-brown coating. This process is known as rusting.

Rusting is the chemical deterioration of iron through its reaction with oxygen in the presence of water or moisture, resulting in the formation of rust, which consists mainly of hydrated iron oxides.

Rust has properties different from those of metallic iron. Its formation is therefore a chemical change, not simply a change in the shape or appearance of the original metal.

Conditions necessary for rusting

Ordinary rust formation requires both:

  • Oxygen: Usually supplied by air or dissolved in water.
  • Water: Present as liquid water or moisture in the air.

If iron is kept completely dry, ordinary rusting is greatly prevented. Likewise, removing access to oxygen inhibits the usual rusting process.

Moisture permits the reactions associated with rust formation. Consequently, iron articles exposed to damp air generally rust more readily than those kept dry.

Why coastal areas encourage rusting

Coastal air often contains considerable moisture, while sea water contains dissolved salts. Salts increase the electrical conductivity of moisture on a metal surface and can accelerate corrosion.

As a result, iron structures near the sea often require more careful protection and maintenance than comparable structures in dry inland environments.

Rusting and corrosion are related but different terms

Corrosion is the broader term for deterioration of metals through chemical or electrochemical reactions with their surroundings.

Rusting refers specifically to the characteristic corrosion of iron and iron-containing materials that produces rust.

Other metals may corrode without producing reddish-brown iron rust. For example, copper can develop a green surface coating, while aluminium commonly develops a thin oxide layer that protects the metal beneath it.

Unlike the protective oxide layer on aluminium, ordinary iron rust is often porous or flaky and may allow corrosion to continue.

How rusting can be prevented

1. Painting

Paint provides a protective barrier between iron and its surroundings. When the coating remains intact, it prevents direct contact with moisture and oxygen.

If the paint is scratched, cracked or peeled away, the exposed iron may begin to rust. Repainting damaged surfaces helps restore protection.

2. Oiling and greasing

A layer of oil or grease limits direct contact between iron and moist air. This is useful for tools, hinges and other suitable iron or steel articles.

Oil and grease coatings can wear away and must be maintained where continued protection is needed.

3. Galvanisation

Galvanisation is the process of protecting iron or steel by coating it with zinc.

The zinc layer acts as a barrier against moisture and oxygen. Zinc is also more reactive than iron and tends to corrode preferentially when the 2 metals are electrically connected and exposed to a suitable environment.

Consequently, galvanised iron can retain some protection even when a small area of zinc coating is damaged. This is an important distinction between zinc coating and an ordinary paint layer.

Galvanised iron sheets, pipes and certain outdoor metal articles are familiar applications.

4. Other metal coatings

Coating iron with a suitable metal such as chromium can produce a protective surface. Such coatings reduce exposure of the iron to corrosive conditions as long as the protective system remains effective.

5. Alloying

An alloy is a material formed by combining a metal with one or more other elements to obtain desirable properties.

Stainless steel contains iron together with chromium and, in many grades, nickel and other elements. Chromium helps form a thin protective oxide layer, making the alloy much more resistant to ordinary rusting than unprotected iron.

Stainless steel is corrosion-resistant, but it is not completely immune to corrosion under every possible condition.

Selecting the correct prevention method

MethodProtective principleExample
PaintingBarrier against air and moistureIron gate
Oiling or greasingProtective surface filmMetal tools and moving parts
GalvanisationZinc coating and preferential corrosion of zincGalvanised iron pipe
Chromium coatingProtective metal surfaceSuitable coated fittings
Stainless steel alloyProtective oxide layer associated with chromiumKitchen utensils

Prelims focus

  • Rusting requires both oxygen and water or moisture.
  • Rust is mainly hydrated iron oxide.
  • Humidity and dissolved salts can accelerate rusting.
  • Galvanisation involves coating iron or steel with zinc.
  • Stainless steel owes much of its corrosion resistance to chromium.
  • Trap: Corrosion can occur in many metals, but rusting specifically refers to iron corrosion.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 6, Physical and Chemical Changes, section 6.3, Rusting of Iron, printed pp. 63–64; NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 1, Chemical Reactions and Equations, section 1.3.1, Corrosion, printed p. 13; NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 3, Metals and Non-metals, section 3.5.1, Prevention of Corrosion, printed p. 54, and section 3.2.1, Reactions of Metals with Oxygen.]

pictures.alt: Ordinary rusting needs oxygen and water. Dry iron does not rust; moist iron rusts, and dissolved salt generally makes it rust faster.
pictures.caption: Moisture and salt change the conditions for rusting.

title: Rusting of Iron: Causes, Conditions and Prevention

What makes water suitable for drinking?

Potable water is water that is suitable and safe for drinking.

Water may look clear and have no unpleasant smell yet still contain disease-causing microorganisms or harmful dissolved substances. Therefore, appearance alone cannot establish that water is potable.

The appropriate treatment depends on the type of contamination present.

Different kinds of impurities in water

Suspended impurities

Suspended impurities are particles that remain mixed with water without completely dissolving. Examples include sand, silt and mud.

These may make water appear cloudy or turbid. Many can be reduced through settling and filtration.

Dissolved substances

Some substances dissolve in water and cannot be seen as separate particles. Common examples include dissolved salts and minerals.

Other dissolved substances, such as excessive fluoride, arsenic or certain industrial contaminants, may make water unsafe at harmful concentrations.

Ordinary cloth filtration or sedimentation cannot remove substances merely because they are dissolved.

Microorganisms

Water may contain bacteria, viruses and protozoan parasites. Some can cause diseases when contaminated water is consumed.

Such organisms may be present even in water that looks completely clear. Suitable disinfection or an effective microorganism-removal treatment is therefore necessary when microbial contamination is a concern.

Basic methods of removing impurities

1. Sedimentation

Sedimentation is the settling of heavier suspended particles at the bottom of a container when water is left undisturbed.

For example, muddy water may become clearer as heavier soil particles settle. However, very fine particles can remain suspended.

2. Decantation

Decantation is the careful separation of the clearer liquid above a settled layer of solids.

After sedimentation, the upper water can be poured off without disturbing the material at the bottom. This method does not remove dissolved salts or reliably eliminate microorganisms.

3. Filtration

Filtration separates particles from water by passing the water through a material with openings or pores that retain some impurities.

A simple cloth or sand filter can remove certain suspended particles. More specialised filters can remove smaller particles and, depending on their pore size, some microorganisms.

Ordinary filtration is not equivalent to disinfection, and not all filters remove dissolved chemicals.

4. Use of alum

Alum can help very fine suspended particles gather into larger masses that settle more readily. This improves clarification of some turbid water.

The use of alum for clarification must not be confused with killing harmful microorganisms. Further appropriate treatment may still be required.

Methods used to reduce disease-causing microorganisms

Boiling

Correct boiling inactivates disease-causing microorganisms, including many bacteria, viruses and protozoan pathogens. It is useful when the main concern is microbial contamination.

However, boiling does not remove dissolved salts, toxic metals or many other chemical contaminants. Evaporation during prolonged boiling can even increase the concentration of some non-volatile dissolved substances.

Chlorination

Chlorination is the use of chlorine-based disinfectants to inactivate susceptible disease-causing microorganisms in water.

Chlorine is widely used in public water treatment. Only suitable products and prescribed quantities should be used, because excessive chemical addition can create problems. Chlorination is not a general method for removing dissolved salts or heavy metals.

Ultraviolet disinfection

Ultraviolet treatment uses suitable UV light to inactivate microorganisms. It works best when water is sufficiently clear for the light to reach the organisms.

UV treatment does not physically remove dissolved salts or chemical contaminants. Unlike chlorine-based disinfection that may leave a protective disinfectant residual, UV treatment does not provide such a continuing residual effect.

Why several treatment stages may be needed

Consider water containing visible mud and potentially harmful microorganisms. Settling and suitable filtration can reduce the suspended solids. An appropriate disinfection method can then address the microbial risk. The treated water must finally be protected against recontamination during storage.

If the original water also contains unsafe dissolved chemicals, these steps alone may be insufficient. A treatment capable of reducing the particular chemical contaminant, or a different safe water source, is required.

Importance of safe storage

Even properly treated water can become contaminated again if stored in a dirty or open container. Clean, covered containers and hygienic dispensing help maintain water quality.

Water purification must therefore be understood as both treatment and protection against recontamination.

Prelims focus

  • Potable water is suitable and safe for drinking.
  • Sedimentation separates heavier suspended particles by settling.
  • Decantation separates the clearer liquid from settled material.
  • Alum helps fine suspended particles aggregate and settle.
  • Boiling and chlorination address microbial contamination but do not remove dissolved salts.
  • Trap: Clear, colourless water is not necessarily safe drinking water.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 6, Chapter 5, Separation of Substances, sections on sedimentation, decantation and filtration, printed pp. 39–44; GCERT, Science, Standard 6, Chapter 9, Methods of Separation in Everyday Life, section on separation methods; NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 18, Pollution of Air and Water, section 18.8, printed p. 248; Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, How Water Treatment Works, sections on filtration and disinfection, and Household Water Treatment, consulted 3 November 2026.]
